Labor lawyer running for Iowa attorney general. He is a lifelong Iowan and a father who says he has spent his career taking on corporations over stolen wages, outsourced jobs, and workplace safety. He says that work has covered tens of thousands of Iowans. He says he will go after wage theft, worker misclassification, and unpaid overtime. He says he will hold corporations accountable for cheating families, work with prosecutors on violent crime, and protect seniors from scams and nursing-home safety failures. He says the office is the one that can fine corporate polluters who contaminate air and water, and that it should focus on Iowa rather than national political fights.

State senator running for attorney general. He says he is a state senator and a longtime litigator and mediator who has passed 134 bills since 2019, on subjects that include water, energy, education, health care, and criminal justice. He says he is running because Texans need a lawyer who will use the office for the public. He says he will defend individual rights, go to court against federal actions he calls illegal, and investigate public corruption without regard to party. He says he will enforce consumer-protection and competition laws against price gouging, scams, and unfair competition. He says he will work with local district attorneys on identity theft, cybercrime, Medicaid fraud, and human trafficking, and help secure the border without tactics he says violate the Constitution.

U.S. representative running for another term. Nathaniel Moran's campaign says he grew up in East Texas, attended West Point, and finished degrees in Russian, business, and law at Texas Tech. He says his politics come from Christian faith, family, and a duty to defend liberty and the Constitution. He highlights his work on the Ways and Means Committee, which covers taxes, trade, Social Security, and Medicare, and on a House committee focused on the Chinese Communist Party.

Poverty-law lawyer running for Congress in eastern Kentucky. He says he has had an underdog, high-volume poverty law practice for 44 years and has worked with several nonprofits. U.S. representative for Alaska The campaign says Nick Begich was born in Anchorage, studied entrepreneurship at Baylor and earned an MBA at Indiana University, then worked at Ford before returning to Alaska in 2004 to build businesses. Former federal prosecutor running for attorney general. His campaign calls him a lifelong Oklahoman and a career prosecutor, not a politician. U.S. representative running for another term. Pat Fallon's campaign says he is a military veteran and business owner who served on a city council and for years in the Texas House and Senate. Green Beret and businessman representing North Carolina's 10th District. Kansas state representative and chair of the House Elections Committee, running for secretary of state. Republican nominee for Congress from Indianapolis. Deschutes County commissioner running for Congress in Oregon's 5th District. Candidate for Missouri's 1st Congressional District. Dentist and U.S. representative for Arizona's 9th District. His campaign says he practiced dentistry for 25 years, first won a House seat in 2010, and is in his sixth term. He says he would extend Interstate 11 between Phoenix and Las Vegas and would not cut military health and retirement benefits to fund other programs.

Former Maine governor running for Congress The campaign says Paul LePage left home as a child, finished school, built businesses, served as a Republican mayor, and then as Maine's governor. He says he is running for Congress to bring that same direct style to Washington. He says he will cut wasteful spending that he argues drove inflation, and he pledges to protect Social Security and Medicare. He says he will finish a border wall, end illegal immigration, and lower taxes and red tape so Maine gets more jobs. He says he will defend the Second Amendment and veterans' health care and benefits.

Iowa secretary of state serving a third term. He is a small-business owner from Linn County and a former state senator and mayor of Cedar Rapids. He says he made it easier for service members overseas to vote, started online voter registration, and brought voter ID to Iowa. He says he started the Safe at Home program for survivors of violence and has pushed election cybersecurity and ballot access for Iowans with disabilities. He says business-filing changes have cut bureaucracy and sped processing for Iowa companies, under a slogan of easy to vote and hard to cheat.

He says families are paying more for housing, groceries, and energy, and that many young people are unsure they can afford to stay. He says a governor should make daily life more affordable and answer to residents rather than to either major party.

Missouri legislator running for Congress on a conservative platform. His campaign says he is done accepting the status quo and wants to carry the fight he led in Jefferson City into the U.S. House, alongside President Trump. He says he will defend the Second Amendment in Congress after helping write Missouri laws he calls among the strongest gun protections in the country. He says he is fully opposed to abortion, wants Planned Parenthood's federal funding ended, and cites votes to lengthen Missouri's waiting period and to notify parents of minors. He supports a border wall, full funding for ICE, and deportation of people he calls criminal illegal aliens, and he says grocery and gas prices have to come down.

U.S. representative for Arkansas's 1st District The campaign says Rick Crawford grew up in an Air Force family, served as an Army explosive-ordnance technician, and earned an agriculture business degree from Arkansas State University. He founded the AgWatch radio network, was first elected in 2010, and now chairs the House Intelligence Committee. He says addressing the federal debt is his top priority and that he wants permanent spending controls. He says he wants to keep an overzealous federal government off people's backs. His campaign also invites supporters to join him in lowering taxes, growing the economy, and standing up for conservative values.

Army veteran and school board member running for Congress in Wisconsin's 8th District. His campaign says he has served in the U.S. Army, in business, and on a school board. He says he is running to represent northeast Wisconsin and help people solve problems. He says the campaign is focused on affordability, which he describes as helping families meet their needs without constant financial stress. He says accountability means leaders who show up, listen, and act transparently. He says results means real improvements in people's lives, and that he wants leadership that brings people together.

Founder of Jackson Healthcare, running for governor. His letter says he built Jackson Healthcare, which operates in all 50 states, helps care for more than 20 million patients a year, and generates over $3 billion in annual revenue. He describes a childhood in public housing and five foster homes, raised by a mother struggling with alcoholism. He says he is running to cut the income tax, freeze property taxes, and lower costs so Georgia is the most affordable state. He says he stepped in when China threatened the U.S. antibiotic supply, and that Governor Brian Kemp called him during COVID to help supply doctors and nurses. He says he will also work to secure the state.

U.S. representative for Washington's 2nd District. His family has lived in northwest Washington for more than a century; he grew up in Arlington as the son of a union power-line worker and a mother who raised eight children, and he worked his way through Pacific Lutheran University. He says his votes are aimed at lowering costs, bringing federal investment home, and building an economy that works for more people. He says he will hold the administration and ICE accountable, combat fentanyl, and protect reproductive freedom. He also lists more access to health care and support for veterans, and he serves as the lead Democrat on the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee.
District 2 · U.S. House · West Virginia · Republican

U.S. representative for West Virginia's 2nd District. Riley Moore's office says he started as a welder in a mining operation, later earned degrees from George Mason University and the National Defense University, served in the West Virginia House, and was state treasurer before Congress. He lives in Harpers Ferry with his wife Mina and their three children and serves on House Appropriations. He says that as treasurer he divested state funds from BlackRock over its support for ESG policies and helped other states push back on those policies. He says he also helped pass and administer the Hope Scholarship and Jumpstart Savings programs.

Candidate for Congress campaigning on Utah family costs and limits on political self-dealing. His priorities page says elected officials should serve the public, and that Washington needs new faces rather than career politicians. He supports tax credits for businesses that offer six weeks of paid maternity leave, and he wants federal housing funds tied to local zoning reform. He says he will sponsor a bill requiring age verification for social media users 16 and older. He also calls for a ban on congressional stock trading, term limits, and an end to Citizens United.

Candidate for governor Risa Lombardo says she is running for governor to speak for people she believes the major parties ignore. She says she has been registered with both major parties and spent most of her life as a Democrat. Her issues page lists the Green Party call to cut the military budget sharply and to move from fossil fuels to renewable energy. That page also demands a living wage and a stronger safety net. It calls for public financing of elections, open debates, and voting systems she describes as more representative.
District 15 · U.S. House · New York · Democratic

U.S. representative for New York's 15th District. His campaign says he was raised in the Bronx by a single mother earning minimum wage and grew up in public housing with leaks, lead, and unreliable heat. It says that at 25 he became the city's youngest elected official and the first openly LGBTQ elected official from the Bronx. He says he will fight for health care, housing, schools, and jobs, and stand up for immigrants, seniors, and young people. He says he will work to protect neighborhoods from gun violence and make the Bronx safer, more decent, and more affordable.

Business researcher running for Congress. Ritesh Tandon's campaign says he has lived in the Bay Area for 26 years and is a research fellow at UC Berkeley's Haas School of Business. It says his grandfather fought in India's independence movement, and that this history shapes his view of public service. He says he would cut everyday costs for groceries, utilities, transportation, and insurance by increasing competition and cracking down on junk fees. He says he would speed housing permits, help first-time buyers, and expand workforce housing near jobs and transit. He says he would lower out-of-pocket medical and drug costs, make job training cheaper, and oppose new layers of taxes and fees.

U.S. representative running for another term. Ro Khanna's campaign says he grew up in a middle-class immigrant family in Bucks County, Pennsylvania, studied economics at the University of Chicago, and earned a law degree at Yale. It says he later taught economics at Stanford and represents Silicon Valley after winning a House seat on his third try. He says his platform is Medicare for All, taxes on billionaires, good jobs in every town, and no foreign wars. He also campaigns on free child care, free college and trade school, and a path to homeownership by age 35. He says technology should put humans first, and he lists reproductive rights, a living wage, and expanding Social Security among his priorities.

California attorney general running for re-election. Rob Bonta, the attorney general, says he is the people's lawyer and that the job is to hold lawbreakers accountable, including people in positions of power. His campaign is asking voters to re-elect him. He says he is defending California's gun laws, including the assault-weapons ban, and expanding programs that take guns from people barred from having them. He says health care is a human right and that he is defending the state's reproductive-care laws and coverage expansions. He says he is taking polluters to court, especially where pollution falls on poorer communities, and pursuing employers who steal wages.

U.S. representative for Pennsylvania's 8th District. Rob Bresnahan Jr. is a fifth-generation northeastern Pennsylvanian who took over his grandfather's union electrical company at 19 and was elected to Congress in 2024. He serves on Transportation and Infrastructure, Small Business, and Agriculture. He says he supports securing the border, stopping wasteful spending, cutting taxes, and backing law enforcement against fentanyl. He says he will protect Social Security and Medicare without raising the retirement age or cutting benefits, and that he wants more jobs in the region.
District 8 · U.S. House · New Jersey · Democratic

U.S. representative for New Jersey's 8th District. His campaign says he was born and raised in Hudson County and elected to the House in 2022. He says his priorities are working families, organized labor, infrastructure, climate, and reproductive choice. He says he is running again to defend freedoms and not back down, including over immigration enforcement. He says the district shares values of respect, hard work, and a chance for everyone to succeed. He says he serves as a regional whip and as northeast vice chair of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee.

Iowa state auditor running for governor. He says Iowa now has the worst economy in the nation, public schools that have slipped to the middle of the pack, and the country's fastest growth in cancer. He says he has proposed mandatory prison for theft of taxpayer money every year since he became state auditor, and that a 2023 law let agencies hide documents from that office. He says he would ban stock trading by the governor, legislators, and other covered officials, require personal financial disclosures and blind trusts, and make violations carry mandatory prison time. He says anyone who steals more than $10,000 in taxpayer dollars should face mandatory prison, a ban on doing business with the state, and loss of taxpayer-funded retirement and health benefits. He says he would restore powers taken from the auditor in 2023, extend whistleblower protections beyond state employees, and require annual audits, tuition limits, and income limits for the private-school voucher program.

U.S. representative for Virginia's 1st District. He says he was adopted at eight months after time at the Children's Home Society of Virginia, raised in Henrico County by a World War II veteran and a public-school teacher, and worked jobs from groceries and a cannery to fishing boats. He studied biology at Virginia Tech, earned a master's in public health from the University of North Carolina, and a Ph.D. in public policy from Virginia Commonwealth University. He says he lives in Montross and spends the week driving between home and Washington. He says Washington should lower the cost of groceries, power, housing, health care, and child care, keep taxes down, produce more American energy, and cut regulations that make it harder to build and hire. He says he supported tax relief that locked in and doubled the Child Tax Credit, raised the standard deduction to $31,500 for families, and ended tax on qualifying tips and overtime. He also says he backed tax provisions that help small businesses invest and let seniors keep more of their Social Security checks.

Pastor and nonprofit leader running for Congress The campaign says Robb Ryerse is a pastor and nonprofit leader who has lived in Springdale for 20 years with his wife, Vanessa, and their four children. He first ran for Congress in 2018 and says he is running again so working families are heard. He says he will not take corporate PAC money and that the campaign is funded by neighbors. He says a representative should show up for town halls and answer questions in the district. He says he wants good jobs, safe neighborhoods, strong schools, and a government that works for families rather than a party.

Nevada County supervisor running for Congress. Robb Tucker's campaign says he was born in Nevada County, holds degrees from Pepperdine and Wheaton, and led a family mobile-home business before it was sold. It says he was elected to the Board of Supervisors in 2024 and has focused there on public safety, small businesses, and local quality of life. He says federal rules written for big cities stall rural work on forests, water, housing, and roads, and he wants early county consultation and rural-impact reviews. He says Washington should back border enforcement, fentanyl prosecutions, and equipment and hiring for rural sheriff's offices. He says homelessness funding should require treatment and fewer unsheltered encampments, and that federal land managers should help clear hazardous fuels before wildfires.

Member of Congress from Alabama's 4th District The campaign describes Robert Aderholt as a pro-life member of Congress who has spent more than a decade on abortion policy and who treats rebuilding the economy as his first priority. It points to growth in aerospace, defense, agriculture, and manufacturing in north Alabama and says that work is not finished. He says he wants further tax cuts, less regulation, and jobs brought back so the country is less dependent on critical goods from China, Russia, and other rivals. He supports more U.S. energy production, including opening the Keystone pipeline, and broadband so rural small businesses can compete. The campaign calls him one of the leading pro-life members of Congress and says he has worked to defend life and promote alternatives to abortion.

Candidate for governor who says he would follow a public vote before he signs or vetoes. His site, which he calls the Farmer Servant Movement, says he is Robert Brooks and that the other candidates in the race have already held office. He says he would publish what people decide and what action follows. He proposes an app in which registered voters would weigh in on bills, pardons, and policy before he acts, and says he would follow the majority. He says schools should put parents, teachers, and students first and show measurable gains. He says he would respect property rights and working families, and that he has no tolerance for pay-to-play politics.

Dedham resident running again for Congress. Rob Burke's site says he was born in Boston in 1956, grew up in Milton, worked in telecommunications, and later delivered packages in Boston before running for this seat in 2022 and 2024. He says he is running in 2026 as an American Citizens First candidate and would serve one term. He says his Boxer Works plan would make Brockton a manufacturing hub for aerospace, defense, medical devices, and other goods, with a stated goal of 21,000 jobs and Junior ROTC training. He says voting should require citizenship and voter identification, and he calls for a pause on immigration programs from H-1B visas to temporary protected status. He says he would cut taxes, bring manufacturing back, support law enforcement, and shift health coverage toward catastrophic insurance people buy themselves.

U.S. representative and former mayor running for another term. Robert Garcia's campaign says his mother brought him to the United States without English or a formal education, and that a 1980s immigration law let the family apply for permanent residency. It says he became a citizen in his early twenties and later served as mayor of Long Beach. He says he supports Proposition 50 and sees defending democracy against the far right as Congress's most important job. He says he supports the Green New Deal and is leading a transportation version of it to electrify public transit. He says every young adult should have a tuition-free college or trade program, undocumented families should have a path to citizenship, and everyone should have health care and housing.

D.C. Statehood Green Party nominee for mayor He describes himself as a native Washingtonian, an advocate, and an eco-socialist, and as the Gen-Z candidate in the mayor's race. He says his agenda uses a Human Life Standard to judge whether a policy improves daily life. He says he would use artificial intelligence to improve city budgeting, shorten permits, and update government technology. He says that work would speed public services, including public Wi-Fi, and publish real-time performance dashboards. He says the platform covers affordable housing, economic opportunity, public safety, education, and transparent city government.

Independent candidate for the U.S. Senate. He says he will not take campaign donations, from a party, a business, or a PAC, so that money cannot buy his vote. He asks people to give to local nonprofits instead and to spread his campaign by word of mouth. He says he would seek an Accountability Act so constituents can be polled on major issues and officials must explain votes that go against that result. On daily costs, he says communities should buy food together, use simpler construction to make housing cheaper, and rethink a health system that charges cash patients and insured patients very different prices. He says he supports the Second Amendment for law-abiding people, wants an open debate about modern limits, and says immigration enforcement should use due process.

Candidate who calls himself Family Man Murray. His campaign says he would improve health, restore what he calls the we in wealth, and respect both states' rights and civil rights. He pledges to donate his post-tax congressional salary to Virginia charities until individual taxes no longer pay that salary. He says he would press Congress to stop taxing individual income, including tips and Social Security, and to bring 80 percent of overseas military forces home by 2032. He says technology should not surveil, deceive, or silence people, and that he would shield Virginians from data centers they do not want. He says he would fix family law, protect speech, religion, association, equal opportunity, and privacy, and govern by the Golden Rule.

Retired soldier and Democratic nominee for Florida's 15th District His campaign says he was born in Baltimore in 1979, the second of four children, and grew up with a single mother in poverty. He joined the Army the day after he turned 18, served 21 years including two tours in Iraq and one in Afghanistan, and retired in 2018. He says he took an oath to the Constitution and is still keeping it. He says he would protect Social Security and support Medicare for All. He says he would protect vote by mail and the environment, and oppose a data center when the community does not want it. He says his priorities also include housing, food, utility costs, and disaster preparedness.

Businessman and former election judge running for Wyoming secretary of state. His campaign says the office has to follow rules that build trust, fairness, and accuracy, and that he would carry out the constitutional and statutory duties of the job. He says he would use the office against sham corporations and people who misuse privacy laws to disadvantage Wyoming businesses. He says fair elections depend on county clerks and local volunteers, and that he would act quickly if the process goes wrong. He says he would investigate securities violations, including cryptocurrency scams, and refer criminal matters to the proper authorities.

State treasurer running for secretary of state. His campaign says his background runs from engineering to finance and public policy. It says that as treasurer he invested taxpayer money, cut waste, and modernized systems. He says he is running to defend the vote, the voter's voice, and the family. He says he wants the office to run the most secure elections in the state's history.

Candidate for governor of Tennessee. He says he was born and raised in White Pine and has spent his career in education, including a doctorate in school leadership. He says he is running so family concerns are treated as real priorities, and that his faith is a private foundation for stewardship rather than something he would impose. He says his schooling background is meant to guide how the state spends on teachers and on student results. He says Tennessee needs community mental-health systems that can handle a crisis and support students. He says the state budget should be managed within the state's means.

Former Chicago alderman · attorney · Democrat until he switched parties Known as Bob Fioretti. Has run for Chicago mayor, Cook County board president, and Cook County state’s attorney. He says the office spends too much time on national lawsuits and too little on crime and corruption in Illinois. Push state’s attorneys to prosecute violent crime more aggressively. He says the office should “represent the victims of crime.” “Restore the rule of law” and “break this cycle of crime and corruption.” He says he agreed with only three of Raoul’s suits against the Trump administration, and that Raoul is rarely the lead plaintiff when many Democratic states sue together.

Former state legislator and Army veteran running for Congress in Maryland's 6th District. His campaign says he is a lifelong Marylander who grew up here, raised a family, started businesses, and owns a farm. It says he is a U.S. Army veteran who served in the Maryland legislature and passed ballot measures on property taxes and county term limits. He says he would cut wasteful spending and the deficit, support police, and hold people who commit crimes accountable. He says he would lower taxes and regulation so jobs stay in the United States and in Maryland. He opposes making the District of Columbia part of Maryland and says only American citizens should vote in American elections.

School board member and small-business owner running for Congress. Robin Littau's campaign says she is a Republican, an Enterprise Elementary school board member, a Coast Guard veteran, and the owner of a cleaning company and a local magazine. It says she was born in South Dakota, later settled in Redding, and is running to represent the 2nd Congressional District. She says she would cut excessive regulation, support local control, and require more responsible federal spending. She says she would change immigration policy, including citizenship requirements, and back a parental bill of rights against mandates. She says she would support law enforcement, stronger deterrence against people who harm children, small businesses, and constitutional rights.

Ralston school board member running for U.S. Senate in Nebraska. Her campaign says she grew up in Nebraska, serves on the Ralston school board, and has two sons in those same schools. She says years of door-knocking convinced her that people want someone who answers the phone after Election Day. She says costs are too high and that she wants good jobs so people can build a life where they already live. She says health care should not stand between a family and a secure future. She calls for fully funded public schools and housing people can actually live in, especially for working families, rural towns, small businesses, farmers, and ranchers.

U.S. senator from Kansas and an OB-GYN from Great Bend. Roger Marshall's campaign says he spent twenty-five years delivering babies and has spent nearly a decade writing bills he ties to Kansas households. He highlights farm bills on fertilizer costs, whole milk in schools, and interstate sale of state-inspected beef. He points to hospital and Medicare bills on prior authorization, price transparency, Medicare Advantage, and lasting telehealth. He also lists border legislation, energy production including ethanol and natural gas, aerospace work in Wichita, and water conservation over the aquifer.

U.S. representative running for another term. Roger Williams's campaign says he grew up in Fort Worth, played baseball at TCU and in the Atlanta Braves system, and has run a family car dealership and cattle operation for more than 50 years. It says he was Texas secretary of state and was elected to Congress in 2012. He says his priorities are lower taxes, less government, cutting spending, defending the border, listening to generals, the Tenth Amendment, and standing with Israel. He says that as a business owner he opposes taxes and regulation that hurt small businesses, and that he chairs the House Small Business Committee.

Republican candidate for Mississippi's 2nd District. His campaign says he served 20 years on active duty, then worked in cardiac and thoracic surgery in Mississippi, including helping start a cardiac surgery program in Vicksburg. He says he later founded a manufacturing company, Buck Warrior Enterprises. He says he stands for free enterprise, limited government, individual liberties, national defense, and traditional values, and he lists himself as pro-life and pro-Second Amendment. He says Mississippi needs more business opportunity and less government interference and red tape. He supports congressional term limits and says the general-election campaign is about economic growth, secure borders, voter integrity, and constitutional rights.

U.S. representative for Kansas's 4th District and a former state treasurer. Ron Estes's campaign says he is a fifth-generation Kansan and an engineer who served as Sedgwick County treasurer and Kansas state treasurer before Congress. He serves on the House Ways and Means Committee, and he and his wife Susan live in Wichita with their three children. He highlights tax reform, free and fair trade, retirement security, lower health-care prices, Wichita's aviation industry, and the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement. He says he will defend the Second Amendment, stand for the sanctity of life, secure the border, and support the military and veterans. He says he is working to rein in federal spending, balance the budget, and ease regulations on Kansas farmers, workers, and small businesses.

Retired Army officer and small-business owner running for Congress. Ron Russell's site says he is a Maine native and West Point graduate who served 30 years in the Army as an Airborne Ranger and Special Forces-qualified Green Beret. He says that after retiring in 2006 he helped build a defense business past 150 employees and moved back to Maine in 2021. He says Maine cannot afford more federal taxes on top of a high state and local burden, and he wants tax relief he ties to the law he calls the Big Beautiful Bill made permanent, with inflation adjustments and a larger work-linked earned-income credit. He says energy independence is the main way to strengthen the economy and lower fuel, grocery, and heating-oil costs, and that renewable energy should be a choice rather than a mandate. He says he supports vetted legal immigration and assimilation, and that securing the border against unlawful crossings should come first.

Trial lawyer, Army veteran, and former law-firm chairman. His campaign says he grew up on a Minnesota dairy farm, served in the Army, and is a partner in a national litigation firm, where he was chairman from 2019 to 2024. He says he is running because the state needs an attorney general focused on crime, fraud, and the rule of law. He says fighting fraud and protecting tax dollars would be a top priority, and that he would try to stop fraud before it starts. He says seniors, families, and small businesses need a consumer-protection lawyer who will take on scammers and powerful companies. He says he would enforce the law and put public safety ahead of political headlines.

U.S. representative running for another term. Ronny Jackson's campaign says he is a retired Navy rear admiral who was White House physician to three presidents and chief medical adviser to Donald Trump. It says he represents a large Panhandle and North Texas district and serves on Armed Services, Agriculture, Foreign Affairs, and Intelligence. He says his focus is national security, support for farmers and ranchers, and keeping the country strong and free. The campaign describes that work as defending Texas families in Congress.

U.S. representative for Connecticut's 3rd District The campaign says Rosa DeLauro has represented Connecticut's 3rd District since 1991 and is the ranking Democrat on the House Appropriations Committee, which she chaired in 2020. It says she wrote the Paycheck Fairness Act and worked on the child tax credit. She says she has shifted spending toward education, health care, climate, and community safety rather than billionaires and corporations. The campaign says she has brought more than $70 million to the district for local projects since 2021. It says she has worked to improve schools, cut taxes for middle-class families, protect pensions, and encourage jobs in Connecticut.
District 9 · U.S. House · New Jersey · Republican

Clifton council member running for Congress in New Jersey's 9th District. Her campaign says she is a mother, wife, educator, cancer survivor, and Clifton councilwoman who left the Democratic Party. She says she is running because working-class families in Passaic, Bergen, and Hudson counties have been forgotten. She says she would lower the cost of living, create good-paying jobs, and keep neighborhoods safe. She says she will oppose large spending bills that fuel inflation and support tax cuts for working families. She says affordable American energy brings down the cost of groceries, transportation, housing, and utilities.

Former governor and former attorney general of North Carolina. His campaign says he was born and raised in Nash County, practiced law in Rocky Mount, served in the legislature, and was attorney general for four terms before he was elected governor. He says that as governor he worked with both parties on jobs and on a Medicaid expansion. He says he is running to lower the cost of food, health care, energy, child care, and housing. He says the middle class feels out of reach while the largest corporations and the richest Americans have gained wealth. He says that as attorney general he prosecuted crimes and went after scammers, predatory lenders, drug companies, and big banks.

Retired Army major running for Congress. Rudy Recile's campaign says he is a retired Army major with more than 26 years of service, a small-business owner, and a former Agriculture Department employee. It says his last post brought him to Fairfield and that he and his wife stayed in California after he retired in 2014. He says public-school results are too low and wants a return to reading, writing, and math, with parents told what their children are taught. He says education money should follow the child, including tax credits for private school, home school, and extra tuition. He says Congress should move long-stalled veterans disability bills, and he wants election systems open to verification so no one company controls voting.

U.S. representative and fourth-generation Hoosier from South Bend. He says he was born and raised in South Bend, earned a business degree from Indiana University South Bend and an executive MBA from Notre Dame, and represents Indiana's Second District. He describes himself as a Christian, a family man, and a conservative. He says Washington is stuck in gridlock and bureaucracy, and that he wants limited government, individual liberty, and fiscal responsibility. He says power should sit with the people rather than an expanding federal bureaucracy, and that he would cut red tape and restore a balance between federal and state power. He says his priorities in Congress are shrinking the federal bureaucracy, restoring fiscal responsibility, and making sure veterans get the care and benefits they earned.

Member of Congress from Idaho The campaign says Russ Fulcher has voted to fund a border wall, toured the border, and backed a balanced-budget amendment and a one-subject-at-a-time bill. It presents him as a conservative delivering on issues important to Idaho. He supports full enforcement of immigration law and an orderly legal process, and he opposes illegal immigration. He opposes breaching the lower four Snake River dams, which he says supply hydropower, irrigation, and a path for Idaho wheat to market. He says he is pro-life, will defend the Second Amendment, and wants local communities to have more say over Idaho's forests, minerals, and energy.
District 7 · U.S. House · South Carolina · Republican

U.S. representative for South Carolina's 7th District. Russell Fry's office says he represents the Grand Strand and Pee Dee. He put himself through the University of South Carolina and the Charleston School of Law, practiced law along the Grand Strand for more than a decade, and served seven years in the South Carolina House, including as chief majority whip. He says that as a state legislator he fought for lower taxes, less government, and pro-Second Amendment legislation. He says government decisions fall hardest on families living paycheck to paycheck, and that he wants to leave the country better than he found it.
Secretary of State · North Dakota · Democratic

News anchor and Republican nominee for Florida's 7th District His campaign says he is an Emmy-winning news anchor who hosted the weekly show Orlando Matters, and that a consumer segment he created returned money to residents and took on Social Security and consumer-protection cases. He and his wife, Tasha, raised their two boys in Seminole County. He says he has lived in Florida for 20 years, 14 of them in the 7th District. He says Congress should keep taxes low, cut regulation, and pursue American energy independence so family costs come down. He says health care should be affordable and patient-centered, with expanded health savings accounts and clear prices from hospitals and insurers. He says he supports parental rights and school choice, and protection for Volusia County's beaches.

Connecticut state senator He says he was born in Norwalk, raised in Greenwich, and earned an economics degree from Northwestern University before working in energy, agriculture, and shipping. He also served on Greenwich's Representative Town Meeting and its Energy Efficiency Committee. He says he co-authored a 2023 bill to disclose hidden utility taxes. He says he co-authored a 2025 bill to reduce public-benefits charges on electric bills. He says he authored a 2024 bill supporting municipal home rule.

U.S. representative for Pennsylvania's 7th District. Ryan Mackenzie joined Congress in 2025 after serving in the Pennsylvania House and says he is a lifelong resident of the district. He serves on Education and the Workforce, Foreign Affairs, and Homeland Security, and chairs the Workforce Protections Subcommittee. His campaign says he is focused on seniors and Medicare, lowering costs, and banning members of Congress from trading stocks. He says his committee work is aimed at protecting workers and the district's interests on education, foreign affairs, and homeland security.

Former naval officer running for secretary of state. He says he served more than a decade as a naval officer, led sailors overseas, worked on defense policy in the Senate, and helped develop officers at the Naval Academy. He says he is back in Iowa and running to do the elections job without being a partisan warrior. He says the job is to make sure every eligible Iowan can vote and that elections are fair and secure. He says he has met county auditors across the state and wants to be a partner they can trust. He says trust in the office depends on keeping politics out of the work.

Lieutenant governor Sabina Matos's campaign says she is lieutenant governor and grew up working in Providence. She says her focus is making the state a place where families can get ahead. She says she is pushing legislation to stop grocery price gouging and to bring more grocery stores into neighborhoods that need them. She says she has fought for affordable housing since her time on the Providence City Council. She says she will defend reproductive freedom and the right to vote, and that every Rhode Islander should feel safe at home.

U.S. representative running for another term. Salud Carbajal's campaign says he immigrated from Mexico at age five, grew up in a mining and then a farmworker family, and earned degrees from UC Santa Barbara and Fielding Graduate University. It says he served in the Marine Corps Reserve, including during the 1991 Gulf War, and on the Santa Barbara County Board of Supervisors before his election to Congress in 2016. He says he is running to lower the cost of living and expand opportunity for working families. He says he would defend immigrant communities from immigration raids he calls extreme. He says he would protect the local environment, pointing to his opposition to new offshore oil drilling and work on a county climate plan.

Democratic candidate for Montana's 1st District. His campaign says he is a Forest Service smokejumper and a vice president of his union local, raised by a nurse and a public-school teacher. He worked his way through the University of Montana and says he has organized for public education, libraries, health care, and constitutional freedoms. On housing he calls for federal investments matched to the shortage, zoning reform, a ban on hedge funds buying homes, and restoration of the first-time homebuyer credit. On health care he says every Montanan should have the choice of Medicare that covers dental, vision, and hearing, and that Medicare should negotiate all drug prices. He wants Citizens United overturned, lower contribution limits, a ban on members of Congress trading stocks, and a stop to former members becoming lobbyists.

Pastor and business leader running for Congress. Sam Gallucci's campaign describes him as a business leader, pastor, and community servant running in the 26th District. It says he is offering results rather than more talk from Washington. He says he would back law enforcement, first responders, and community-based prevention. He says he would defend the coast, forests, and reliable water with practical, science-guided solutions. His site also lists the cost of living, parent-centered education, homelessness, immigration, and veterans among his priorities.

U.S. representative running for another term. Sam Liccardo's campaign says his first term has focused on homelessness, the cost of living, and the Constitution, and that both chambers have passed housing bills he wrote. It says he has also worked on health-care costs and local funding for housing, infrastructure, and public safety. He says he is trying to make housing more affordable, including by turning vacant buildings into homes and protecting low-income families from homelessness. He says he has written bipartisan bills to lower health-insurance premiums and bank fees. He says he wants technology used so more Americans benefit from innovation, and he is working to protect constitutional rights.

Working-class organizer running for Congress. Samantha Mota's campaign says she is a 27-year-old mother and a working-class candidate, not a career politician. She says she is running to make government more accessible and to reduce corruption and the influence of money. Her site lists economic security, community-based projects, immigration reform, and universal health care among her priorities. She says she wants politics to be more affordable and more open to participation.

Attorney running for attorney general. Samuel Kane Sr.'s campaign says he is an attorney with decades of experience who was not born in New Mexico and later made it home. It says he is a cyclist, a pilot, and married to Jessica, his business partner. He says he would challenge license-plate reader surveillance that tracks people without a warrant. He says methamphetamine and fentanyl are driving a crime crisis and that he would back officers on those cases. He says he would scrutinize data-center projects and utility rate increases, and that environmental laws should be enforced so the land stays intact.

State legislator running for lieutenant governor. Sandra Jauregui says she worked during the Great Recession to help Nevadans stay in their homes and has served in the Legislature. She says she survived the October 1 mass shooting. She says her legislative work includes more affordable housing, a cap on insulin costs, lower health-care costs, and protections for wages and benefits. She says the shooting led her to push gun-safety laws. She says she is running for lieutenant governor to take that record statewide.

Respiratory therapist and disability worker running for Congress. Sandra Van Scotter's campaign says she grew up in a working-class family of eight children and spent decades as a respiratory therapist before moving to Ridgecrest in 2014. It says she now supports adults with developmental disabilities, and that her own son uses the state's regional-center system. She says she supports Medicare for All and would work to reverse health-care cuts she argues will hurt Medi-Cal recipients, people with disabilities, and seniors. She says disability services are underfunded and too hard to navigate, and she would bring that experience to Congress. She says immigration policy should combine a path to legal status for longtime workers with border security, and she wants water policy that serves Valley farms and residents.

U.S. representative for Georgia's 2nd District, seeking another term. He says he is in his sixteenth term and is the top Democrat on the Appropriations Subcommittee on Agriculture. A Morehouse College and Emory Law graduate, he served in the Georgia House and Senate before his election to Congress in 1992, and he enlisted in the Army in 1969. He says the district's farms, including its peanut crop, need disaster aid, market access, rural broadband, and a farm bill that supports food security and local food networks. He supports the Affordable Care Act, more accessible care, and funding for veterans' medical care, and he highlights Fort Benning and Albany's Marine Corps Logistics Base. He describes his goal as jobs, education, safe communities, a clean environment, energy independence, and a strong defense, pursued alongside a balanced budget.

U.S. representative running for another term. Sara Jacobs's campaign says she is a third-generation San Diegan who graduated from San Diego public schools. It says she has worked in policy roles at the State Department, UNICEF, and the United Nations. She says the country must act on climate change and on gun violence in schools and communities. She says she is fighting for housing people can afford, health care as a human right, and access to reproductive care. She says that in Congress she is working so every child has the same opportunities.

Vermont secretary of state, first elected in 2022. Her campaign says she served 18 years in the Vermont House before this office, including work that made universal vote-by-mail permanent for general elections. She says the office registers businesses, runs elections and campaign-finance disclosure, licenses professions, and preserves state and local records. She points to a universal voter guide, a new election management system, and the Safe at Home program for people facing domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking. She says civic education, including a Kid Governor program and visits to schools, is a priority of the office.

U.S. representative and the youngest woman ever elected to Congress from Maryland. She says she learned her work ethic in a union household, served six years in the Maryland Senate, and lives in Annapolis with her husband Eric. She says her first term included five bills signed into law and more than 2,000 constituent cases. She says she is working to revoke tariffs that raise prices, expand affordable child care, ease student loans, build more housing, and roll back utility rate increases. She says affordability is personal as a first-time homeowner and young professional with student loans. She says she is also standing up for federal workers, supporting veterans, and protecting the Chesapeake Bay.

Governor of Arkansas Sarah Huckabee Sanders is the 47th governor of Arkansas. She was inaugurated on January 10, 2023, and her campaign says she is the first woman to hold the office and the youngest governor in the country. No 2026 issue list was found for this candidate.

U.S. representative for Delaware The campaign says Sarah McBride, a Wilmington native, represents Delaware's at-large House seat after serving the state's 1st Senate District from 2020 to 2025. As a state senator she highlights the Healthy Delaware Families Act, a paid family and medical leave program, and a Medicaid bill she says brought large new funding to the state.

Small-business owner running for secretary of state. Her campaign says she has an 18-year background as a small-business owner and is running for common-sense leadership. Minister and state senator running for Congress in Iowa's Third District. She says she has met parents who ration medicine so their children can eat and seniors who skip meals to pay heating bills, and she wants to crack down on price gouging and end tariff policy she says raises family costs. She says she would expand the Child Tax Credit and Earned Income Tax Credit, provide paid family and medical leave, and eliminate junk fees and surprise medical bills. She says she would stand up for hardworking Iowans and protect their freedom, paycheck, and future rather than chase partisan wins.

Former federal prosecutor running for attorney general. Her campaign says that after the September 11 attacks she went to law school and spent more than a decade prosecuting terrorism, cybercrime, drug trafficking, and corruption cases. It says she later served as chief of staff at the Drug Enforcement Administration and is a mother of four. She says the attorney general should enforce the law by prosecuting crime, and that safety is the office's first job. She says she would get people who are homeless or sick off the street in a humane way. She says she would go after corruption and fraud, and that she would work with police and district attorneys on repeat offenders, hate crimes, and fentanyl cases.

District attorney. His campaign says he is a seventh-generation Mississippian from Columbus, a husband and father of two, and that he has been a prosecutor, a judge, and a district attorney. U.S. representative for Wisconsin's 5th District, seeking another term. He says he will help small businesses, support law enforcement as the son and father of officers, and defend the right to life and the Second Amendment. He says he is pushing back on socialism and on bureaucracies he says are out of control.

U.S. representative for Florida's 18th District His campaign says he is a conservative Republican, Navy veteran, and small-business owner in his third term. He says he would secure the border, strengthen defense, and restore fiscal discipline in Washington. Entrepreneur and Libertarian candidate for governor He says he is a Boca Raton entrepreneur running with his wife, Regina, and that they live with homeownership and rising insurance costs. Business owner running for secretary of state. His campaign calls him a business owner and a conservative and says he is running to restore confidence in elections and in government services. Mayor of Boca Raton and Republican nominee for Florida's 25th District His campaign says he was born in Miami Beach, grew up in Fort Lauderdale, and has lived in the district for 40 years. He and his wife, Bella, have two children. He says he voted seven times to lower Boca Raton's tax rate and has pledged not to raise taxes. He says he would keep the border and national defense strong, cut waste, and work with President Trump. He says he supports a term-limits amendment and a ban on members of Congress trading stocks.

California state senator running for Congress. Scott Wiener's campaign says he has worked for San Francisco for 28 years as a deputy city attorney, supervisor, and state senator, and that he has written a large body of state law. It says he is a gay man who helped build the city's LGBT Community Center and chaired the Senate Budget Committee. He says he would abolish ICE, ban face coverings that hide agents, let people sue federal officers, end private immigration prisons, and create a path to citizenship. He says he would push a plan to build 8 million homes in a decade, including social housing and a larger housing tax credit, paid for by reversing parts of corporate and high-end tax cuts. He says he would pass the Equality Act, defend Medicaid and the Affordable Care Act on the way to Medicare for All, and increase federal transit operating funds.

He supports solar, wind, and nuclear power, including the Palisades plant, and says he would protect the Great Lakes and drinking water.

Libertarian business owner running for secretary of state. Sean Vadney says he was born in a Denver suburb, raised by a working-class single mother, and has worked in politics for almost seven years. He says he is a Libertarian and a business owner running for secretary of state. He says every voter, of any party, should feel secure, and that voting should include checks against fraud. He says Coloradans across parties are worried about election integrity and that he wants people to feel confident when they cast a ballot. He says starting and keeping a business should be easy and affordable, and that he has run into red tape and high costs as a business owner.

Former president of the University of Montana. His campaign says he was raised by two public-school teachers, joined the military at 18, graduated from West Point, studied at Oxford as a Rhodes Scholar, and served in Iraq as an infantry officer and as a Green Beret. He says he would work to lower health care, housing, and energy costs. He says he would answer to Montanans rather than party leaders or corporate donors, and that he wants to end dark money and ban congressional insider trading.

Civics teacher and Democratic nominee for Florida's 3rd District His campaign says he teaches 7th-grade civics at Lincoln Middle School in Gainesville. He says he would protect Social Security by raising the payroll tax cap to $250,000 without cutting retirees' payments. He says every American should have affordable health care so a family is not bankrupted by getting sick. He says he would expand child care with a sliding-scale subsidy and tax large corporate purchases of single-family homes so more families can buy a house.

Green Party candidate for secretary of state. His campaign says he was born and raised in Baudette, studied political science near St. Cloud, and has worked in cooperatives, businesses, and nonprofits, including as a union steward. He says he now works for the Land Stewardship Project. He says he would keep paper ballots, early and absentee voting, and same-day registration, and he wants Election Day to be a paid state holiday. He says he would expand voting rights to Minnesota residents regardless of U.S. citizenship or a criminal conviction. He says he would end the legal split between major and minor parties and support ranked-choice voting for state executive offices.

Energy investment banker running for Congress. Shaun Finnie's campaign says he grew up on a farm, was the first in his family to finish college, and earned degrees in economics, law, and business. Retired Army brigadier general and cattle farmer running for Georgia's 14th District. U.S. representative and fourth-generation Oklahoman. Small-business owner running for governor of Colorado. He told the Fort Collins Coloradoan he runs Scooter's Autoservice, a towing and recovery business. He says he would lower the burden on working Coloradans and put their interests ahead of parties and special interests.

Former ironworker and U.S. representative from Boston. Libertarian candidate for governor. Stephen Villee is the Libertarian nominee. Former television news director running for Congress. Candidate for governor of California. Steve Hilton says California has become more expensive because insiders built a system that protects the political class. He says he will clear the rules and fees that keep young families from buying starter homes. He says every student should read by third grade, every school should offer skills training, and the annual $800 small-business tax should end.

House majority leader representing southeast Louisiana. Secretary of state of Minnesota. His campaign says his family fled persecution in Lithuania and settled on the Iron Range, and that his father's illness later made voting in person hard. State representative running for Congress. He says he would support local businesses, defend educational opportunity, and improve local infrastructure.

Libertarian candidate for the U.S. Senate. He says he is a retired independent insurance adjuster who studied political science at UCLA and has been active in the Libertarian Party since 1979. Milwaukee resident running for Congress in Wisconsin's 4th District. His campaign says he was born and raised in Milwaukee, graduated from North Division High School in 1978, and studied at UW-Parkside and MATC. It says his father and uncle owned a grocery store, and that he has spent almost 30 years delivering for local businesses while singing in church and alumni choirs. He says schools, graduation rates, and a justice system he calls uneven have declined, and that he wants justice applied equally. He says aging lead water lines and poor drinking water need action, not more talk. He says he will stand up for the district on taxes and representation and try to restore neighborhood quality of life.

U.S. representative and former pastor. His campaign says he served as a pastor for nearly 10 years, spent 16 years in the Michigan House, and later led a community foundation and worked for the Moody Bible Institute. He says less power in Washington and more in families, businesses, and local communities will strengthen Michigan. He says his focus is job creation, higher incomes, and a federal government that lives within its means. He says lowering drug costs, protecting people with pre-existing conditions, and fighting addiction are health-care priorities. He says he has voted to support veterans, religious freedom, the Second Amendment, and a right to life.
Treasurer on the Kane County list and the Will County list. The lists do not state a party. A vote counts only where this declaration was filed.
District 26 · U.S. House · New York · Democratic

U.S. representative for New York's 26th District. His campaign says he grew up in a working-class Buffalo family, began as an occupational therapist, and served 14 years in the state Senate before winning a 2024 special election to the House. It says he serves on Veterans' Affairs and Homeland Security, where he is ranking member of the emergency-management subcommittee. He says he is fighting cuts to veterans' services and to health care for families, seniors, and people with disabilities, and working to lower the cost of living in Western New York. He says that as a state senator he pushed a multiyear transportation building plan, protections for organized labor, record school funding, abortion rights, LGBTQ students, and stronger gun laws.

Governor of Oregon, seeking another term. Her campaign says she began her career advocating for families in need and still treats that as the job. It says her first term has focused on the cost of living, homelessness, and schools. She says her plan is to make life more affordable and create more economic opportunity. She says she wants every student to succeed. She says she would defend what makes Oregon distinct while continuing work on homelessness and schools.

Candidate for the U.S. Senate and an Army veteran. He says he served as an Army officer, was trained on weapons, and deployed to the Persian Gulf. He describes himself as a capitalist who wants an economy that rewards work and strengthens Idaho's middle class. He says he will seek a constitutional amendment limiting senators to two terms and House members to three, ban members of Congress from trading individual stocks, and close tax loopholes he says the wealthy and corporations use. He says he will protect health-insurance tax credits, require upfront medical prices, and build on a housing bill that limits large investors from buying single-family homes. He says he will oppose selling Idaho public lands, vote against new federal bans on firearms or magazines, and staff Customs and Border Protection while updating legal visas for farm work.

U.S. representative and Army veteran. His campaign says he was born and raised in Michigan, served 22 years in the Army, including Iraq, and used the GI Bill to graduate from Western Michigan University. He lives in Charlotte with his wife Ashley and their four children, and he says he previously served eight years in the state legislature. He says taxpayer subsidies for large corporations are the wrong use of public money, and that infrastructure, tax and regulatory reform, and a lower cost of living matter more. He says he opposes defunding police, wants schools focused on teaching and safety, and has signed a taxpayer-protection pledge to lower the tax burden. He says he would finish the border wall and give border agencies the tools to stop illegal crossings, and he describes himself as pro-life.

U.S. representative running for reelection in Oklahoma's 4th District The campaign says Tom Cole has spent his career in service to Oklahoma. In Congress, it says, he has focused on national defense, taxpayers, small businesses, and Native American and tribal issues. Announcing his 2026 reelection bid, Cole says a Republican Congress and White House have secured the border, brought inflation down, and cut taxes, including on tips, overtime, and Social Security. He says Republicans passed energy legislation to create jobs in Oklahoma and raised military pay, expanded VA services, and increased law enforcement funding. He says he is running to support America First policies, national security, and continued work at Fort Sill and Tinker Air Force Base.

U.S. senator from Arkansas Tom Cotton is a U.S. senator who grew up on a cattle farm in Yell County, graduated from Harvard and Harvard Law School, and served as an Army infantry officer with combat tours in Iraq and Afghanistan. His campaign says he chairs the Senate Intelligence Committee. He says he wrote the RAISE Act, helped pass the Laken Riley Act, and has a voting record he describes as fully opposed to illegal immigration. He says he cast a decisive vote for a large middle-class tax cut, ended the Affordable Care Act tax on Arkansans, and worked to lower energy and health-care costs. He says his Armed Services work and his relationship with President Trump brought billions in defense investment to places including Pine Bluff, Fort Ebbing, and Little Rock.

House majority whip representing Minnesota's 6th District. Born in 1961 and raised in Minnesota, he says he was first elected in 2014 and now serves as majority whip. He says he brings a Minnesota work ethic and common-sense leadership to Washington. He says he is fighting high grocery, gas, and electricity costs and backed a tax law that keeps cuts in place and ends taxes on tips, overtime, and adds relief for seniors. He says he led the border bill H.R. 2 and supported the Laken Riley Act so people in the country illegally who commit crimes are deported. He says he supports the SAVE Act's proof-of-citizenship requirement, school choice, and ending the U.S. Department of Education.

U.S. representative running for another term. Tom McClintock's campaign says he is running for re-election in a district covering the Sierra foothills and Central Valley counties. It says he serves on the Budget and Natural Resources committees, chairs the Federal Lands Subcommittee, and previously spent 22 years in the California Legislature. He says the national debt is the country's greatest danger and wants a balanced-budget amendment, yearly review of mandatory spending, and no spending that Congress has not authorized. He says environmental review and lawsuits have blocked routine forest thinning, leaving overcrowded federal forests to burn. He says he has pushed legislation to speed removal of dead timber, replanting, and management that reduces catastrophic fire.
No 2026 issue list was found for this candidate.

Former member of Congress running again in Virginia's 5th District. His campaign says he previously delivered emergency economic relief after the 2008 crash, voted against bailing out Wall Street, and cast a vote he says delivered affordable care and kept rural clinics open. He says he has rejected lobbyist and corporate PAC donations and is endorsed by End Citizens United. He says his first priority is lowering costs by ending tariffs that raised grocery bills, ending the Iran war he says raised gas and fertilizer prices, and stopping deals he says are bankrupting the country. He says he will keep fighting until every family can afford health care, child care, housing, and a secure retirement. He says he would ban dark money and insider trading and pursue people he says are tied to the Epstein files and to theft from the treasury.

Toledo business owner running for secretary of state. His campaign says he was born and raised in Toledo, has worked in printing since 1985, and has owned NorthCoast Print Mail Marketing since 2017. It says he has also led Polish-American community groups in northwest Ohio and has run before for the Toledo school board and for Lucas County clerk of courts. He says the office has been used as a gatekeeper for the two major parties and should treat every candidate equally, including on ballot access. He says election security and access can go together, with accurate voter rolls, secure systems, and procedures that do not change at the last minute. He says the office should publish election and campaign-finance information more clearly, and should make business filings faster and less burdened by red tape.

West Texas businessman running for Congress. Tom Sell's campaign says he is a fifth-generation West Texan who earned agribusiness and law degrees at Texas Tech and worked for Congressman Larry Combest, including on the 2002 farm bill and crop-insurance reform. It says he then co-founded a Lubbock firm with Combest and is running to stand with Donald Trump. He says his platform is a strong border, energy dominance, the Second Amendment, and protections for unborn life. He says he would champion agriculture, West Texas values, and national defense, and oppose what he calls Sharia law.

Member of Congress and former small-business owner running for governor. His campaign says he grew up on a dairy farm in western Wisconsin, worked his way through UW-River Falls, and with his wife ran Wilderness Cruises in the Northwoods for two decades. It says he also tended a dam on the Willow Flowage for 29 years. He says he has balanced budgets and worked on border security, and that he is running so Wisconsin families can still own a business and raise children. He says he will stand up to unelected bureaucrats and fight for farmers and other workers. He argues that another four years of the current leadership in Madison would raise taxes and shrink opportunity.

U.S. senator and former college football coach Tommy Tuberville is a U.S. senator from Alabama and a former college football coach, best known for his years at Auburn. His campaign says he was elected to the Senate in 2020 and is running for governor at the end of that Senate term. He says men should not compete in women's sports, that critical race theory and diversity, equity, and inclusion programs do not belong in schools or government, and that no tax money should pay for abortions. He says he will cut taxes, cut waste, and work to bring manufacturing jobs back to Alabama. He says he will expand school choice across charter, magnet, private, public, and home schools, and that parents should control a child's education.

Beaver County sheriff running for Congress in Pennsylvania's 17th District. Tony Guy is a lifelong Beaver County resident who served 26 years with the Pennsylvania State Police and has been sheriff since 2016. He says he is not a career politician and is running to take local values to Washington. He says he will back law enforcement, fund and finish a border wall, deport people he calls criminal immigrants, and stop fentanyl trafficking. He also wants pro-growth policies for small business, manufacturing, natural gas, and agriculture, and less federal regulation and spending.

Former Navy combat aviator and attorney running for Congress. Raised in LaGrange, he says he attended the U.S. Naval Academy, flew the F/A-18 Super Hornet, and completed three combat deployments. He says he is running because Rich McCormick stopped showing up for the 7th District. He says members of Congress should not trade individual stocks or hide behind omnibus bills nobody reads, and he lists a ban on congressional stock trading as a way to rebuild trust. He points to child-care costs, families priced out of homeownership, and full-time work that no longer covers a household, and he says he has a plan to lower those costs. He says he will fight to lower health costs, protect coverage, and hold the insurance industry accountable, arguing that premiums were allowed to double.

Republican candidate who says government should work for the people it serves. His campaign says Northern Virginia sits at the center of national security, the federal workforce, and the economy, and that families there feel rising costs and strained infrastructure. He says he is running to focus on solutions. He says his priorities are lowering energy costs, creating jobs, and protecting small businesses. He names the Energy Affordability and American Power Act, the American Jobs and Opportunity Act, the Small Business First Act, the Safe Communities and Secure America Act, and an American Health Freedom Plan.

U.S. representative and businessman for Wisconsin's 8th District. His campaign says he is an America First businessman who spent three decades starting and running companies in northeast Wisconsin, and that he ran because career politicians made empty promises. He says he is a political outsider. He says illegal immigration surged under the Biden administration and that the border still has to be secured against crime and human trafficking. He says he will cut federal spending, get government out of the way of American energy, and keep the military strong. He says he will protect farmers and other agricultural producers by reducing regulations so they can succeed.

Former Kansas lieutenant governor The campaign says Tracey Mann served as Kansas's 50th lieutenant governor. A fifth-generation Kansan, he was born and raised on his family's farm south of Quinter and worked in the fields and feed yard with his grandfather, father, and brother. He says life begins at conception and that he will protect unborn life. He says he will be a voice for farmers and ranchers and wants rural communities to thrive, not just survive. He supports the Second Amendment and says the southern border should be secured with a wall.

Former Alaska attorney general Treg Taylor joined the Alaska Department of Law in 2018 as deputy attorney general for the civil division, became attorney general in 2021, and served until August 2025. Before state service he was counsel at McKinley Capital Management and senior counsel at ASRC Energy Services. He says Alaska should unleash its energy resources and reform permitting so families pay less for energy and businesses can hire. His campaign says that as attorney general he helped drive crime to a 40-year low and cut sexual assaults by 25 percent, and that he will keep pressing prosecutions. He says the state should pay the largest Permanent Fund Dividend it can afford and protect the dividend in the constitution.

U.S. representative for Mississippi's 1st District. His official biography says he won a 2015 special election, lives in Saltillo with his wife, Sheila, and their three children, and served 39 years in the Mississippi Army National Guard, retiring as a major general. Before Congress he was district attorney for the 1st Circuit, covering seven north Mississippi counties. On his issues page he says the primary role of the federal government is to keep the country safe at home and abroad, and he points to his National Guard service. He says the Second Amendment means the right to keep and bear arms shall not be infringed, and that law-abiding gun owners should be protected. He supports an all-of-the-above energy strategy and says Washington should not pick winners and losers. He also says he will keep pushing agriculture policies that encourage rural development.

Retired Army colonel running for Congress. Trever Nehls's campaign says he served 33 years in the Army, rising from infantryman to colonel with deployments to Iraq, Afghanistan, and Kuwait. It says he was a Sugar Land police officer and Fort Bend County constable, and that he and his wife are raising three children in the 22nd District. He says he would finish the border wall, end catch-and-release, deport people here illegally, and treat cartels as foreign terrorist organizations. He says he would lower taxes and grocery, gas, and housing costs, back police, and put parents in charge of schools.

Former federal immigration official running for Congress. Trina Swanson's site says she grew up in Hermantown, the daughter of a nurse and a millworker, and spent about 25 years in federal service, rising to director of international operations at U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services. She says she left that career rather than carry out directives she believed were unethical, then came home and started a law firm. She says work should buy a life with dignity and that people should not go bankrupt if they get sick, and she is fighting for affordable health care in rural communities where hospitals can be hours away. She says mining built the region and union jobs built the middle class, and that economic development and environmental stewardship can coexist. She says every young person deserves an affordable path through college, trade school, or an apprenticeship so talent stays in northern and central Minnesota.

U.S. representative for Ohio's 12th District. Troy Balderson says he grew up in Zanesville fixing cars and working on his family's farm, graduated from Zanesville High School, and attended Muskingum College and Ohio State. He says he ran for Congress because of spending, the cost of living, and what children are seeing in and out of school. He says the border should be closed to people who do not enter lawfully, and he wants more agents and technology aimed at cartels, drugs, and illegal crossings. He says government is too big and that the answer is usually to get it out of the way, and he wants shop classes back in schools.

U.S. representative for Louisiana's 2nd District and a former state senator. He says he was the first African American elected to the Louisiana House from New Orleans' 102nd District in 1991 and later the first African American elected to state Senate District 7. He says serving in Congress has been the greatest honor of his life because he is fighting for Louisiana. He says he will keep fighting for fair housing, people with disabilities, criminal and environmental justice, equal pay, and a living wage. He says government should let women make their own health and reproductive decisions, and he wants quality, affordable health care and less student-loan debt. He says he championed the Social Security Fairness Act so teachers, police, and firefighters are not docked by the windfall and pension offsets.

U.S. representative for Montana's 2nd District The campaign says Troy Downing, a Republican combat veteran and businessman, represents Montana's 2nd District and sits on the House Financial Services Committee. Before Congress he was state auditor, securities and insurance commissioner, and a land-board commissioner. He says he advocates lower taxes, less regulation, and policies for economic growth, energy independence, and national security. As insurance commissioner, the campaign says he held companies accountable and worked to keep rates down for families. On the land board, he says he voted for more public-land access and for timber, oil and gas, and agriculture projects.

Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate from Maine. Troy Jackson's campaign says he is a fifth-generation logger from Allagash whose father was a logger, and that he earned an associate degree from the University of Maine at Fort Kent. It says he spent 20 years in the Maine Legislature, six of them as Senate president. He says that in the Legislature he worked to lower prescription-drug prices, pass universal school meals, and expand rural health care. He says he protected union jobs, delivered property-tax relief, and backed strong reproductive-health laws. He says he is running because working families are being squeezed while the wealthiest keep gaining more.
