District 1 · U.S. House · North Dakota · Democratic

Democratic candidate for North Dakota's U.S. House seat. His campaign says he grew up in North Dakota, graduated from Velva High School, enlisted in the Navy, and graduated from the Naval Academy before choosing the Marine Corps. He served as a helicopter pilot and as an infantry officer in Iraq, retired as a major, and later taught science, worked in the Bakken, and counseled Job Corps students in Minot. He says Americans pay the world's highest health-care prices and that people should not have to choose between care and rent or food. He says he will protect Social Security and put North Dakota seniors first, and he opposes raising the retirement age. He says profitable corporations and the ultra-wealthy should pay a fair share, and that rural towns need support for public schools and farm markets, with Congress asserting its power over tariffs.

President of the Kansas Senate, running for governor. Ty Masterson's site says he was born and raised in Butler County, has been married to Marlo for 30 years, and has six children and seven grandchildren. He says he won local office in Andover more than twenty years ago and has stayed in public office since. He says that as Senate president he led a tax-cut package he calls the largest in Kansas history, and that he wants lower taxes, safer streets, and a government that answers to the people who pay for it. He proposes a Homeowners Bill of Rights aimed at property taxes and a stronger voice for taxpayers. He offers a Kansas Ratepayer Protection Pledge against higher costs he says outside interests would push onto families, farms, schools, hospitals, and small businesses.

Attorney and independent candidate for U.S. Senate. His campaign says he grew up in Rolling Fork, the son of a tractor driver, chopped cotton as a teenager, and was the first in his family to finish high school and attend college. He says he is running as an independent because he believes neither party is listening. He says health care is a right and that he supports the Medicare for All Act. He says he is not tied to either party or to lobbyists who profit from the current insurance system. He says his own father's untreated diabetes, and the loss of work and a vehicle that followed, is why the issue is personal.

Contractor and small-business owner running for Congress. Tyler Bass's site says he is a contractor, small-business owner, and former licensed life and health insurance agent who has worked since he was 10, including roofing, siding, and factory jobs. He says he started a business with a $250 paycheck after college. He says he will secure the border, support ICE, and remove people who are here illegally no matter how long they have been here, and cut H-1B loopholes so jobs go to Minnesotans. He says he will fight Washington's hand in local property taxes and will not vote to ban AR-15s, restrict magazine capacity, or add new hurdles for law-abiding gun owners. He says fraud that robbed children with autism and Minnesota taxpayers has to be confronted, and that his opponent has not spoken up about it.

Mattapoisett Select Board member running for Congress. Tyler Macallister's site says he is a lifelong Cape Codder who settled in Mattapoisett in 2001 with his wife, Cindy, and has served more than 20 years locally, including five terms on the Select Board. He describes himself as an advocate for sustainable fishing and the working waterfront. He says he will defend the fishing fleet with practical, science-based rules and oppose industrial wind farms in fishing grounds and data centers that drain the grid and water. He says he will take on mandates and federal spending that raise grocery, fuel, and housing costs, and he backs an all-of-the-above energy policy aimed at lower bills. He says he will back local police and child-safety standards, and protect the benefits veterans and seniors have earned.

U.S. representative for Oregon's 4th District, seeking another term. Her campaign says she comes from a union family, worked as a waitress and for 25 years in the bicycle industry, and later served as Oregon labor commissioner and as House majority leader. It says she now represents the 4th District and focuses on working families. She says people who work should be able to find a union job, buy a home, and start a family in Oregon, and she highlights paid sick leave, a higher minimum wage, apprenticeships, and the PRO Act. She supports universal preschool, a cap on child-care costs, paid family and medical leave, lower prescription prices, and restoring enhanced Affordable Care Act premium tax credits while still pushing for universal health care. Her campaign also points to reproductive health care, protecting vote-by-mail, and a shift toward cleaner energy.
District 4 · U.S. House · North Carolina · Democratic

U.S. representative for North Carolina's 4th District. She says she grew up watching her parents work multiple jobs and first ran to speak for students who were overlooked, especially Black and brown children. She describes herself as a mother, a public servant, and a lifelong North Carolinian. She says Donald Trump is the biggest threat to democracy the country has faced, and she points to court briefs, impeachment support, and a boycott of his joint address. She wants to limit ICE, ban agents from wearing masks, require body cameras, and she says she introduced articles of impeachment against Secretary Kristi Noem and voted against a Homeland Security bill that funded ICE. She calls health care a universal right, supports Medicare for All and extended Affordable Care Act subsidies, and says she will protect abortion access and focus on schools, jobs, and a fair shot.

Consultant running for Congress in Ohio's 8th District. Vanessa Enoch says she is a public-policy and management consultant who has led Cultural Impact, LLC for more than 25 years and has worked as a community organizer. She says she is running because families who are doing everything right still feel squeezed. She says affordability means updating the rules that drive up health care and housing costs and expanding places to rent or buy near jobs. She says data-center companies, not working families, should pay for the power lines and grid upgrades they need, and that those facilities should not pollute neighborhoods or replace farmland.

U.S. representative running for another term. Veronica Escobar's campaign says she is a third-generation El Pasoan who served as a county commissioner and county judge before Congress, including work to open the border's only children's hospital. It says she was the first woman elected to represent El Paso in the House. She says health care is a right and supports Medicare for All, an insulin cap, and Medicare coverage for dental, vision, and hearing. She says she would protect Social Security from cuts or privatization and seek fair, lasting immigration reform. She says she is working on climate policy, fair wages, and reproductive rights.

Independent candidate for U.S. Senate. Veronica Fernandez says she has lived in New Jersey her whole life, is married to a Navy veteran and electrician, and co-owns a small commercial electrical business. She says she previously worked as an insurance underwriter. She says Congress has to be cleaned up so big money and special interests stop controlling it, and that the people who created the problem will not be the ones to fix it. She says she has lived with the same costs for health care and groceries, help for a child with special needs, and trying to save for retirement. She says she is not a lawyer and is not connected to people in power, and that new leadership has to come from outside the circle that created the problem.

U.S. representative running for another term. Vicente Gonzalez's campaign says he has worked for South Texas since 2017 and focuses on practical results for the 34th District. He says he is focused on lowering everyday costs, protecting seniors' benefits, and defending women's access to health care. He says he supports public schools, veterans' services, and affordable health care families can rely on.

Attorney and Democratic nominee for Florida's 19th District His campaign says he has owned and managed Arias Law Firm since 2002 and previously served as a staff attorney for the Lee County and St. Lucie County school districts. He says he would cut Veterans Affairs red tape and protect Medicare and Social Security for seniors. He says he would expand economic opportunity and invest in infrastructure and education. He says he would protect clean water and improve access to affordable health care.

Candidate for governor of Colorado. Victor Marx says he is a husband, father, and community worker who has supported veterans and people in crisis, and that he founded organizations to do that work. He says he is running to restore trust and put families' safety and costs first. He says he will back law enforcement and make public safety a first priority. He says he will lower the cost of living, change housing policy, cut taxes, and push for good-paying jobs. He says government should answer to taxpayers rather than to special interests.
District 2 · U.S. House · Rhode Island · Republican

Marine Corps veteran and businessman running for Congress. His campaign says he is a U.S. Marine Corps veteran, father, and grandfather who built a business supporting working families for three decades. He says he is running to protect the next generation and is not a career politician. He says his housing plan would speed homebuilding, empower local trades, and send federal housing funds to working families, first-time buyers, and veterans. He says he would work to bring investment home for ports, manufacturers, and skilled trades so Rhode Island has good-paying jobs from entry level to executive level. He says elections should be easy to vote in and hard to cheat, with accurate voter rolls and open processes.

Independent candidate for governor of Tennessee. He says he is a Navy veteran, a retired Ford journeyman, a longtime volunteer firefighter, and an active armed guard and river captain. He says he founded Save the Cumberland and answers to Tennessee taxpayers rather than to donors. He says he would fund law enforcement, restore gun rights and voting rights to people with nonviolent felony convictions, and change bail and plea practice. He lists property-tax reform, English as the only official language, and keeping lobbyists out of health-care decisions. He says he opposes a Duck River dam at Columbia and opposes new data centers, and he wants campaign spending limits and term limits.

Working parent running for Congress in Tennessee's 4th District. Her campaign says she is a working-class mother from rural Tennessee who grew up across the South before landing in Lincoln County. She says she previously built a short campaign while working full time after learning her opponent might otherwise run unopposed. She says her SAFE plan covers community safety, including rural hospitals and gun violence, and bringing down everyday costs, including pre-K and a path to homeownership. She says she would protect privacy, keep the federal government out of personal decisions, secure the border with a fair immigration process, and end federal marijuana penalties. She also says corporate taxes should encourage American investment and that data centers should be accountable to communities.

Businesswoman and U.S. representative for Indiana's 5th District. Born in Ukraine, she says she immigrated after meeting her husband, became a U.S. citizen, and worked from bank teller to CPA, finance executive, and business owner. She served in the Indiana Senate and was elected to Congress in 2020. She says the national debt should be cut by reducing spending and balancing the budget, not by raising taxes on citizens. She says the legal immigration process is too long, expensive, and bureaucratic, and that a stronger work-visa program should serve the national interest. She says health-care costs need more transparency, competition, and consumer choice, and that politics should be a duty rather than a career.

State representative running for lieutenant governor. The site identifies her as a state representative running for lieutenant governor because people across Texas asked her to. She says the Senate needs a presiding officer who takes ideas from the whole chamber. She says neighborhood public schools should be well funded, and that tax money should not go to vouchers for religious schools. She says families deserve clean drinking water and reliable energy, and that corporations should not come ahead of those families. She says Texas needs more homes and apartments, limits on tax increases, and health coverage that includes preventive care and specialists.

U.S. representative running for another term. Vince Fong's campaign says he was born and raised in Bakersfield, earned degrees from UCLA and Princeton, and spent nearly a decade as district director for Kevin McCarthy. It says he was elected to the House in 2024. He says domestic energy production should lower costs for families and small businesses while the country still protects the environment. He says farmers need more storage and conveyance and fewer rules that send water out to sea. He says border enforcement should come before other immigration changes, and he opposes new gun limits on people who follow the law.
District 1 · U.S. House · West Virginia · Democratic

Former teacher and community advocate running for Congress. His campaign says he is a public servant, former teacher, and community advocate running to speak for working-class West Virginians. He says he is running to unseat Carol Miller. He says the minimum wage has stayed at $8.75, jobs have disappeared, hospitals are closing, and more families are struggling to put food on the table. He says the state's members of Congress voted for cuts to SNAP, Medicaid, Medicare, and veterans' benefits, and that the biggest cuts take effect after this election.
District 5 · U.S. House · North Carolina · Republican

U.S. representative for North Carolina's 5th District. Her campaign says she is a mother and grandmother and the granddaughter of Italian immigrants who came seeking opportunity. She says the right to life and religious liberty are central to her work. She says she would ban elective abortion later in pregnancy, end federal funding of abortion, and protect people punished for living out their faith. She says immigration changes should secure the border and uphold the law, and that Americans need the Second Amendment to defend themselves. She says patients, including people with preexisting conditions, should have lower costs and more choices, and she opposes Medicare for All.
District 25 · U.S. House · New York · Republican

Monroe County legislator running for Congress in New York's 25th District. Her campaign says she is a county legislator and educator focused on taxpayer-first budgeting and on older adults, people with special needs, caregivers, veterans, and local businesses. It says she wants to deliver for Monroe and Ontario counties. She says she would support community policing and prevention programs, and expand vocational and technical education tied to good careers. She says she would grow good-paying jobs, ease the burden on working families, fix roads and bridges, and expand broadband. She says health-care billing should be transparent so families are not surprised by the cost of care.

Cincinnati native and business leader running for governor. His campaign describes him as a husband and father who has spent his career turning business ideas into results. He says he is running to restore opportunity and keep the American Dream available in Ohio. He says the state should be more affordable, with lower taxes, lower energy bills, and more money in household budgets. He says children should get a world-class education. He says the state should protect neighborhoods, revive cities, and put unity ahead of division.

Green Party candidate for governor and former Marine Walid Hakim's campaign says his family moved to South Carolina in 1985, that he attended Lexington High School and Newberry College, and that he left college to enlist in the Marine Corps after Iraq invaded Kuwait. It says he has worked as a police officer, restaurant owner, and in other jobs. His listed platform objectives are a 100-year plan, education reform, law-and-order reform, and land reform. The site says the Green Party campaign is meant to widen the debate in a state long dominated by one party.
No 2026 issue list was found for this candidate.

U.S. representative for Ohio's 8th District. Warren Davidson's campaign describes him as a West Point graduate and former Army Ranger who served in the 75th Ranger Regiment, the 101st Airborne, the 3rd Infantry Division, and the Old Guard, and as a former manufacturing company owner. He says he wants a government small enough to fit inside the Constitution. He opposes the income tax, argues deficits are driving up prices, and says regulation should be cut back to the minimum needed for fair competition. He says the Second Amendment protects an individual right to keep and bear arms, and he wants people to choose their own mix of health care, coverage, and cost.

President of the Arizona Senate Warren Petersen is president of the Arizona Senate and the Republican candidate for attorney general. His campaign says that in the Senate he defended state laws, opposed mandates he calls unconstitutional, and backed Second Amendment rights. He says as attorney general he will uphold the rule of law and stand with law enforcement to hold criminals accountable. He says he will protect the rights of Arizona families. He says he has worked to keep men out of women's sports and to check government power.

Attorney Wayne Rogers is a Thomasville native and attorney who earned degrees from Samford University and Cumberland School of Law. His campaign says he has worked as a federal prosecutor, spent two decades in private practice, and helped lead Democratic campaigns in Jefferson County. He says the secretary of state should administer elections as an impartial scorekeeper, with partisan politics kept out of who received the most votes. He says he will encourage every eligible Alabamian to vote and expand opportunities to cast a ballot. He says officeholders should put people over party and do what they tell voters they will do.

Candidate for governor of Tennessee. He says he is seeking the job of governor on a campaign that accepts no money and describes itself as nonpartisan. He says the work is to improve jobs, housing, health care, and daily life for Tennesseans. He says he wants health care for everyone, covering both mental and physical health, with the details still to come and with people placed ahead of profit. He says secure housing should be a priority so people can thrive rather than only get by. He says he would push job growth, workforce training, and incentives for businesses that hire and train local workers.
District 5 · U.S. House · South Carolina · Republican

State senator, financial advisor, and business owner running for Congress. His campaign says he is a husband and father of five who represents York County in the South Carolina Senate and works as a financial advisor. He says he is running because Washington is broken and he will fight for President Trump and an America First agenda. He says he has led fights to cut taxes, block wasteful spending, and shrink the power of unelected bureaucrats, including a ban on secret budget spending and more than $2 billion in tax cuts. He says he championed constitutional carry, medical freedom during COVID, school choice, and the toughest fake-meat rules in the nation to protect agriculture. He says he blocked a legislative pay raise in court, secured road funding for York County, and backed property-tax exemptions for veterans.

Governor of Maryland, running for reelection. Wes Moore's campaign says he is Maryland's 63rd governor, a combat veteran who led soldiers in Afghanistan, and a former chief executive of the Robin Hood Foundation. He says his work in office has centered on child poverty, the middle class, and public education. He says he has cut taxes for veterans and middle-class families and wants more Marylanders to be able to afford to live in the state. He points to record spending on public schools and says he wants those schools to be the best in the country. He says public safety is a priority and that homicides in Baltimore are at their lowest level in 50 years.

U.S. representative for Missouri's 1st District. His campaign says the job is to bring federal results home to St. Louis, and it points to infrastructure, public safety, workforce, and neighborhood projects he pursued while Republicans controlled Congress and the White House. He says every family in St. Louis should have a safe, affordable home, and he highlights federal housing grants meant to add supply and lower costs for renters and buyers. He wants Lambert Airport modernized so flights stay on schedule and the region stays connected. He says he fought to expand the Radiation Exposure Compensation Act for North County families sickened by radioactive contamination at Coldwater Creek.

Schaumburg pastor · former financial-services professional · party he founded Degree from Delta State. He worked in banks and insurance, then has pastored in Chicago since 2013. He built the American Center Party for voters who think both major parties have moved to the edges. A finish of 5% would make it an established party in Illinois. End the Iran war, then ban oil-market speculation by people who never take delivery. He says that would cut prices across the economy. Direct primary care, paying the doctor instead of routing routine care through insurance. Free community college. Keep tariffs off food. Use them to stop dumping that hurts U.S. factories, and negotiate them in private. He says current immigration enforcement has “crossed the line.”

Secretary of the commonwealth, seeking another term. William Galvin's campaign letter says he wants to continue as secretary of state through 2030 and calls himself the longest-serving state elections administrator in the country. He says he is in federal court resisting efforts to limit registration and voting by mail and to obtain detailed personal information about Massachusetts voters. He says he intends to expose and resist federal interference with the 2028 presidential election and the Electoral College. He says he wants a complete Census count in 2030, including group quarters and residents who were not born in the United States, and he lists election integrity, early voting, vote-by-mail, consumer protection, and historical preservation.

Organizer running for Congress in Michigan's 7th District. His campaign says he was raised in East Lansing, graduated from East Lansing High School, and lives in Lansing with his wife. It says he helped found the Sunrise Movement and groups that work on rent and homelessness in mid-Michigan. He says he would lower the cost of living by taxing the wealthy to protect Social Security, building affordable housing, and guaranteeing health care. He wants a 12-month federal pause on new data centers, restored wetlands and rivers, and polluters held accountable. He says he would end what he calls an illegal war on Iran, stop arms sales to Israel and other human-rights violators, and ban stock trading by members of Congress.
District 4 · U.S. House · South Carolina · Republican

U.S. representative who says he entered Congress to bring real reform. His official biography says he is a former prosecutor and small-business owner who served as a state senator, where he fought for accountability and transparency. He is a JAG officer and captain in the South Carolina Air National Guard. He says he ran for office to make a difference and entered Congress in 2019 to bring real reform to Washington. He says he represents Upstate residents on the Financial Services Committee, including its Digital Assets Subcommittee. He says he chairs the Oversight Subcommittee on Military and Foreign Affairs and serves on the Delivering on Government Efficiency Subcommittee.

Attorney General of Connecticut He says he was born and raised in the Hartford area, practiced as a litigator for 18 years, and served 12 years in the Connecticut House, including as chair of the Judiciary and Banking committees. He says he was elected attorney general in 2018. He says he has filed more than 50 lawsuits against federal cuts to police, schools, and medical research. He says he has fought utility rate increases and taken on opioid companies and social-media companies over harm to children. He says he is defending reproductive health care and the state's post-Sandy Hook gun laws.

Former California attorney general running for governor. Xavier Becerra says he is running for governor so families can afford what he calls the California Dream. He points to his record as the state's attorney general challenging the Trump administration. He says health care is a human right and that he would strengthen Medi-Cal and build toward a universal single-payer system. He says he would treat housing as essential infrastructure and build more homes so costs stop rising out of control. He says he would take on insurance, childcare, and grocery costs by standing up to price gouging and unjustified rate hikes.

U.S. representative for Arizona's 3rd District. Her campaign says she represents one of the country's most diverse districts, including Phoenix, and is the youngest woman in this Congress and Democratic freshman class president. She says her first term has focused on costs, immigration enforcement, and reproductive freedom. She says she supports Medicare for All, more affordable housing, free child care, and a federal minimum wage of $25 an hour. She says ICE should be abolished and prosecuted, and that Dreamers, refugees, and asylum seekers need a path to stay. She says she is pushing climate action, public education, and oversight of the administration, including the Epstein investigation.

Community organizer running for Congress. Yolanda Prince's campaign says she is a Tyler native and organizer who was raised to step up rather than wait for change. It says her work has focused on rural opportunity, government accountability, affordability, and health care, including a march to renew the Voting Rights Act. She says she would raise the federal minimum wage to at least $15, raise teacher pay, and protect public schools, special education, school meals, and pre-kindergarten. She supports Medicare for All, higher Medicare payments so rural hospitals can stay open, and lower prescription prices. She says reproductive decisions belong with patients and their doctors, and she wants a less expensive path to citizenship and an end to for-profit prisons.

Candidate for the U.S. Senate. She says her background is in business, accounting, nonprofit work, and community outreach, and that she founded FTP Nonprofit to help local people, including people with disabilities. She says her campaign stresses fiscal responsibility, local communities, public safety, and limited government. She says independent leadership should put hardworking Tennesseans first, with practical steps to strengthen the economy and widen opportunity. She describes a reparations proposal as a fair, lawful, and limited Tennessee-based solution. She says she wants to protect seniors from losing their homes to property taxes.

U.S. representative running for another term. Young Kim's campaign says she was born in South Korea, came to the United States with her family, and was the first Korean American woman elected to represent Southern California in the Assembly. It says she is running for re-election to lower costs and hold Washington accountable. She says she is working to lower the cost of gas, groceries, utilities, health care, and prescription drugs, and to protect Medicare. She says she led a bill to recover taxpayer money lost to fraud after billions were stolen. She says her Assembly work included public safety, help for victims of domestic violence, and resources for veterans and homeless children.
District 9 · U.S. House · New York · Democratic

U.S. representative for New York's 9th District. Her campaign says she still lives in her childhood home in Flatbush, that both of her parents immigrated from Jamaica, and that her mother, Una Clarke, served on the City Council. It says they were the first mother-daughter succession in Council history and that Clarke was first elected to Congress in 2006. She says she has worked to keep Brooklyn affordable for low-income residents, including a 2019 bill to cut rent in subsidized areas and a change to the income formula used for affordable housing. She says she is a cosponsor of a public-housing bill that would fund outstanding capital repairs so residents have a decent home. Her issues page also groups her work under immigration, health care, women and children, LGBTQ rights, and climate.

Former federal prosecutor, Navy JAG officer, and teacher running for Congress. Raised in Lexington, he says he is a ninth-generation Kentuckian who taught eighth grade in the Mississippi Delta, served more than four years as a Navy lawyer, and later prosecuted civil-rights cases and advised Governor Andy Beshear. He says he resigned as a prosecutor because he believed the Justice Department had been politicized. He says tariffs are taxes crushing small businesses and that full-time work should cover a family's bills, including a living wage of at least $15 an hour. He says Medicaid cuts hurt families and hospitals, that one in three Kentuckians relies on Medicaid, and that women should make their own health-care decisions. He says data centers are driving up energy bills and taking farmland without enough local say, and that he left the Justice Department to fight corruption.

Farmer, businessman, and sixth-generation Iowan running for governor. He says he is a father and his own largest donor, and that he answers to his family and to Iowans rather than to corporations. He says he wants Iowa to be a place where his children and grandchildren can stay and build a life. He says he will free Iowa's farmers from a system that leaves the farmer last, and break up monopolies that treat farmers and families as numbers. He says more than 25 percent of Iowa land is owned by out-of-state investors and foreign governments, and he will fight to keep that land in Iowa hands. He says a classroom should be for learning rather than political doctrine, and that anyone who uses a teaching job to push political doctrine will not teach in the state.

Combat veteran and U.S. representative for Iowa's Third District. A sixth-generation Iowan, husband, and father of six, he says he flew more than 700 combat hours after 9/11, served on the National Security Council, and later served in the Iowa House and Senate before winning this U.S. House seat in 2022. He says out-of-control federal spending drove inflation, and he has worked to rein in bureaucracy and stop what he calls tax-and-spend policies. He says he backs law enforcement and a border-security law aimed at drugs, trafficking, and exploitation. He says he fights for a farm bill and for renewable fuels that support Iowa farmers and energy independence.
District 2 · U.S. House · New Jersey · Democratic

Mayor of Cape May running for Congress in New Jersey's 2nd District. His campaign says he was born and raised in South Jersey, built a business in Cape May, and is a father of three serving a second term as the city's mayor. He says he is running as an independent voice for working families. He says he would create good-paying jobs and support small businesses. He says he is fighting for affordable health care and lower prescription costs. He says he wants to address housing costs so working families can stay in their communities.

U.S. representative running for another term. Zoe Lofgren's campaign says she has lived in the Bay Area her whole life, the daughter of a Teamster beer-truck driver and a cafeteria cook, and that she is running for re-election. It says she is the top Democrat on the House Science, Space, and Technology Committee. She says she wants faster research on fusion energy and a stronger federal science agenda on wildfires and flooding. Her campaign points to her work on immigration, health care, technology, transportation, and women's issues. She says the district she represents is unusually diverse, including a large Hispanic population and the country's largest concentration of Vietnamese Americans.

Physician and Navy veteran running for Congress in Arizona's 4th District. His campaign says his parents fled Syria in 1966, he grew up in Wisconsin, served 11 years as a Navy officer, and has practiced medicine in Phoenix for more than 20 years. He and his wife Gada have three children. He says he will rein in spending, let people keep more of what they earn, and cut regulations so small businesses can grow. He supports a balanced-budget amendment and says both parties have spent without regard for whether the country can afford it. He says he will back more resources for border agents and school funding that follows students.
District 2 · U.S. House · South Carolina · Democratic

Air Force reservist and attorney running for Congress. His campaign says he is from Aiken County, served in the Air Force Reserve in transportation logistics, ran track at the University of South Carolina, and earned a law degree from Southern University. It says he spent part of his teenage years in foster care and is 25. He says communities thrive when young people have real options, and that safer communities come from opportunity. He says he would expand workforce training, apprenticeships, and technical education, and strengthen small-town economies. He says he would keep opportunity in South Carolina through small-business growth and local economic development.

South Africa · Local government elections · Wednesday, 4 November 2026 South Africa is electing local councils. This is not an election for president, and it is not the national parliament. Voters are choosing the councils that run cities, towns, and rural areas. The country is divided into 213 municipalities. A municipality is the area one local council governs. Johannesburg and Cape Town are municipalities. So is a rural council whose name you may not know. A province is one of South Africa's nine larger regions, the level above a municipality. The map is those municipalities. Beige means the Electoral Commission has not reported votes there. A color appears only when reported votes have one party ahead. That color is the one the Commission records for the party. It does not stand for a party from another country. This map does not declare a winner. A ward is a smaller piece inside a municipality, closer to a neighborhood or a city district. Ward lines are not drawn. A ward would be colored only from that ward's own reported votes, and those outlines are not matched to this election's file. The Commission publishes voting stations on its own site. This page does not ask for a home address. Reported totals load from the Electoral Commission file. The 213 municipalities These names are the same places as the map, listed from A to Z. Each name is a council, not a candidate. It may be a city, such as Cape Town, a rural area, or a person the council is named for. Open a name to see that council. When two councils share a name, the province is added so they stay separate. Emalahleni in the Eastern Cape is not Emalahleni in Mpumalanga.
